game.name: Below the Crown
game.short_description: Explore the dungeons Below the Crown, in this love letter to Roguelikes, Dungeon Crawlers, and Chess. Prepare for strategy, game-changing spells, psychological tests, and challenges from your fellow players. From the award-winning creators of Duskers & A Virus Named TOM.

other_scores.score: Very Positive, 94.5% of 109 (local snapshot); store page showed 96% of 64

placements.verbal_evidence: I'm going to put this as a high B tier to me, probably more to a lot of people.

commentary.label: Tier list Part 5 (2026)
commentary.summary: Below the Crown is a small, strategy-focused chess roguelike where you command a wizard who summons pieces onto a board inside dungeons. He feels it is the first chess roguelike that truly captures real chess, since good chess play matters more than wild mechanics. Roguelike elements are tiny per-encounter boosts that never overshadow the core chess thinking. He admits he would not play it a lot himself and it may feel repetitive, but he recommends it to chess fans and places it at high B.
praise: Captures the feel of real chess better than other chess roguelikes; chess skill genuinely makes you better
Tutorials teach basic chess tactics like pinning, so players learn something
Smart AI, with gold rewards for strategic plays like checkmates and pins rather than just clearing pieces
Small, simple roguelike elements (easier placement, one-time freeze, one-time transform) fit the game's goals
Limited pieces and a sparse board keep turns slow and deliberate
criticism: Gameplay can feel repetitive, like chess itself
Slow turns and long individual encounters due to heavy thinking
Not a game for everyone; requires careful step-by-step play
He would not personally play it a ton since he is not a strong chess player
unique_points: Roguelike upgrades stay modest so the run is still about playing chess well, even at the final boss
Rewards strategic chess play (checkmate, pins) with gold
Avoids the common trap of piling on crazy rules that erase the chess feel
commentary.quote: it's finally a chess rogike that I could honestly recommend to chess players.
comparisons: Other chess roguelikes (unnamed, one to be discussed afterwards)
design_criteria: Fidelity to core genre (chess): strategy must remain central rather than gimmicks
Roguelike element restraint: small upgrades that do not break the core loop
Reward design: gold for checkmates and pins encourages strategic play
AI quality: smart opponents demand careful thinking
Pacing/run length: slow turns and long encounters, potential repetitiveness
Teaching/accessibility: tutorials on basic chess tactics
Charm/story: frog rooks and fourth-wall-breaking narrative

community.one_liner: A chess-flavoured roguelike puzzle/dungeon crawler from Misfits Attic (Duskers, A Virus Named TOM) where you control a wizard-king, summon and upgrade chess-style pieces, and clear room-sized tactical puzzles.
community.consensus_summary: Players are very positive: Steam shows Very Positive at roughly 94-96 percent across about 110 reviews (103 positive, 6 negative in the local snapshot). It entered Early Access on Nov 10, 2025 and reached 1.0 on Apr 21, 2026 at $14.99, Windows only. The one critic review found (GameGrin, 80/100 or 8/10) calls it creative and fairly balanced but more of a side-activity puzzler than something for long sessions. It is a small, niche title with thin critic coverage, so most of the signal is Steam user reviews. Early Linux crashes and some puzzle-state bugs were reported and at least the Linux crash was later reported fixed. Note: web search quota ran out during research, so Reddit and outlet coverage could not be checked; this summary relies on Steam and one critic review.
best_things: Approachable even for people who are bad at or indifferent to chess: moves are explained, and a danger-tile button shows which squares are threatened
Fair, well-designed puzzles: failures usually feel like your own mistake rather than cheap unfairness (echoed by reviewers and players)
Fresh take on chess roguelikes: you start with no pieces, must move the wizard before placing pieces or casting spells, forcing long-term planning instead of just building an overpowered board
Pieces stay mostly standard with a few restrictive variants, so the game feels 'not too chess but enough chess', with spells, hazard tiles and non-chess pieces adding variety
Retro neon vector/scanline presentation, hum of old electronics and a tense-but-relaxing atmosphere inherited from Duskers
Daily challenge leaderboards, shareable replays and community challenges give short-session replayability
Short runs that can be resumed anytime and multiple win conditions (capture everything or checkmate, board shrinks over time) keep pace brisk
Interesting meta layer: odd psychological-assessment questionnaires and a mysterious emperor narrative that some compare to Inscryption
worst_things: Some players find it shallow or just 'worse than playing chess with generic roguelike mechanics bolted on' (mostly short-playtime negative reviews)
Technical problems at launch/EA: a Linux crash with heavy memory use, invalid game states, a hopper capture not ending a level, a boss turn that would not end, and achievement tracking glitches
Board can feel chaotic once more than about five pieces are in play
Performance issues mentioned in an early negative review
No mid-puzzle restart: failing means leaving the room without bonuses or upgrades (per GameGrin)
Minimal animation; the presentation is stylish but sparse
Narrative is light, especially in the early access build
improvements: Controller support was requested on Steam discussions
A campaign mode built around the Hopper King character was suggested
A way to restart a puzzle mid-room without forfeiting rewards
Bug fixes for stuck boss turns, level-completion triggers and achievements
More depth or content so it holds attention beyond short sessions
Linux stability: early Linux crash with heavy memory use (reported fixed later), although the store page lists Windows only
unique_things: You are a wizard who starts each level with zero pieces and summons them within the wizard's line of sight, unlike drop-anywhere chess roguelikes such as The Rookery
Shrinking board and alternative win conditions remove the need to actually orchestrate a checkmate
Psychological-test questionnaires interleaved with play that affect the runs
Undo tokens, a good-move hint and saved/shared replays make it puzzle-forward and forgiving
Dungeon-crawler framing with RPG-style piece upgrades and spells layered on real chess tactics (forks, pins, skewers)
tedious_or_disliked: Losing a room means losing the run's upgrades from that room with no mid-puzzle restart
Crowded boards with many pieces can become hard to read and calculate
Some situations are perceived as unfair, particularly at the highest difficulty
Players who dislike chess-like thinking find the core loop not engaging
Not a game for long single sittings; better as a second-monitor or between-chores game
divisive_points: Chess as foundation: fans love that chess knowledge is optional, while a few critics say it is simply worse than playing chess
Depth vs shallowness: long-playtime players find deep synergies and builds, short-playtime negative reviewers call it shallow
Session length: praised as bite-sized and flexible, but criticised by the critic as unable to hold focus for a full session
community.reception_notes: Early Access launched Nov 10, 2025 to strongly positive feedback from fans of Duskers and chess games, with praise for the daily challenge leaderboard. 1.0 launched Apr 21, 2026 (publisher Shochiku alongside Misfits Attic) and sentiment stayed Very Positive. A Linux memory/crash bug present in early builds was reported fixed a few weeks after launch by a user. Also distributed in a Humble bundle (Checkmate! A Chess Games Collection) per a Steam review. Metacritic shows no Metascore yet (only one critic review, needs four) and OpenCritic had no findable entry. Steam owner estimate is tiny/unknown (SteamSpy 0-20k). Windows only; Steam Deck/controller support was a player request.
